claims.source: The SCML2 isoform lacking the SPM domain, SCML2B, displayed a predominantly diffuse distribution within the nucleus, which was not affected by the removal of the RBR; however the residual amount of SCML2B that could be recovered from the chromatin fraction was further decreased upon deletion of the RBR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the salt fractionation and microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-G.

claims.claim: The residual amount of SCML2B that could be recovered from the chromatin fraction was further decreased upon deletion of the RBR.
claims.source: The SCML2 isoform lacking the SPM domain, SCML2B, displayed a predominantly diffuse distribution within the nucleus, which was not affected by the removal of the RBR; however the residual amount of SCML2B that could be recovered from the chromatin fraction was further decreased upon deletion of the RBR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the salt fractionation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-G.

claims.claim: The affinity of SCML2 for chromatin is regulated by multiple molecular mechanisms, including binding to PRC1 via the SPM domain, histone marks via the MBT domains, and RNA via the RBR.
claims.source: Together, these results show that the affinity of SCML2 for chromatin is regulated by multiple molecular mechanisms, including binding to PRC1 via the SPM domain, histone marks via the MBT domains, and RNA via the RBR.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the fractionation experiments.

claims.claim: GFP–SCML2A accumulated in the nucleus and exhibited a punctate distribution.
claims.source: Similar to the endogenous SCML2 protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H), GFP–SCML2A accumulated in the nucleus and exhibited a punctate distribution, suggestive of recruitment to specific sub-nuclear compartments, presumably target sites on chromatin (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: GFP-SCML2AΔRBR exhibited a diffuse nuclear distribution.
claims.source: In contrast, GFP-SCML2AΔRBR exhibited a diffuse nuclear distribution (Figure 3F) consistent with its looser association with chromatin revealed by biochemical fractionations (Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The number of intense GFP spots decreased from a median value of 39 per cell for SCML2A to only 5 per cell for SCML2AΔRBR.
claims.source: The number of intense GFP spots decreased from a median value of 39 per cell for SCML2A to only 5 per cell for SCML2AΔRBR (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the quantification shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Deletion of the RBR did not affect the ability of SCML2A to be imported into the nucleus.
claims.source: Deletion of the RBR did not affect the ability of SCML2A to be imported into the nucleus, nor its ability to interact with other protein factors, including the core subunits of the PRC1 complex (see below).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the microscopy data (Figure 3F) and mass spectrometry data (Figure 4A).

claims.claim: Both SCML2AWT and SCML2AΔRBR co-purified with all the components of the canonical PRC1, including RING1A, RING1B, CBX2/8, PHC2/3, and BMI1/PCGF4.
claims.source: Both SCML2AWT and SCML2AΔRBR co-purified with all the components of the canonical PRC1, including RING1A, RING1B, CBX2/8, PHC2/3, and BMI1/PCGF4 (a subunit specific for PRC1.4 [Gao et al., 2012]), suggesting that deletion of the RBR does not affect the ability of SCML2A to interact with PRC1.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Deletion of the RBR does not affect the ability of SCML2A to interact with PRC1.
claims.source: Both SCML2AWT and SCML2AΔRBR co-purified with all the components of the canonical PRC1, including RING1A, RING1B, CBX2/8, PHC2/3, and BMI1/PCGF4 (a subunit specific for PRC1.4 [Gao et al., 2012]), suggesting that deletion of the RBR does not affect the ability of SCML2A to interact with PRC1.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Only small traces of PRC1 components could be detected among the SCML2B-associated proteins.
claims.source: Only small traces of PRC1 components could be detected among the SCML2B-associated proteins, despite the fact that a comparable number of SCML2 peptides were detected in the two purifications (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: SCML2A co-purified with SCMH1 and L3MBTL3, both of which comprise C-terminal SPM domains.
claims.source: SCML2A also co-purified with SCMH1 (the other SCM homolog in humans) and L3MBTL3, both of which comprise C-terminal SPM domains (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Both SCML2A and SCML2B recovered comparable amounts of USP7.
claims.source: As a control, both SCML2A and SCML2B recovered comparable amounts of USP7, in good agreement with previous reports (Sowa et al., 2009) and as we also independently confirmed (Lecona et al. unpublished).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Immunoprecipitation of BMI1 from the chromatin fraction of HeLa cells recovered preferentially the chromatin-associated and SPM-containing SCML2A isoform.
claims.source: In keeping with these observations, immunoprecipitation (IP) of BMI1 from the chromatin fraction of HeLa cells recovered preferentially the chromatin-associated and SPM-containing SCML2A isoform (Figure 4B, compare top and bottom band in lane 4 vs lane 1 or lane 3).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the IP data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Artificial tethering of both SCML2A and SCML2B to an integrated reporter resulted in a dose-dependent repression of transcription.
claims.source: Consistent with the classification of SCML2 as a PcG (and therefore repressive) gene, artificial tethering of both SCML2A and SCML2B to an integrated reporter using the DNA-binding domain of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Gal4p (Vaquero et al., 2004) resulted in a dose-dependent repression of transcription (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Only tethering of SCML2A but not SCML2B caused an increase in BMI1 recruitment to the UAS-containing reporter.
claims.source: However, only tethering of SCML2A but not SCML2B caused an increase in BMI1 recruitment to the UAS-containing reporter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), confirming that the SPM domain is required for interacting with BMI1 and suggesting that SCML2A contributes to PRC1 targeting.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: Recruitment of BMI1 was not necessary for SCML2-mediated repression in the tethering context.
claims.source: On the other hand, recruitment of BMI1 was not necessary for SCML2-mediated repression in this context.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and inferred from the observation that SCML2B represses transcription without recruiting BMI1.

claims.claim: Both the MBT domains and the SPM domain contribute to the repressive activity of SCM in Drosophila.
claims.source: Consistent with this observation, both the MBT domains and the SPM domain contribute to the repressive activity of SCM in Drosophila (Roseman et al., 2001; Peterson et al., 2004; Grimm et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: More than 30% (781 out of 2479 total) of SCML2-enriched regions (ERs) were located in the vicinity (<10 kb) of the transcription start site (TSS) of protein-coding genes.
claims.source: In these cells, more than 30% (781 out of 2479 total) of SCML2-enriched regions (ERs) were located in the vicinity (<10 kb) of the transcription start site (TSS) of protein-coding genes (Figure 4D), consistent with a role for SCML2 in gene regulation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: SCML2 targets were significantly enriched for gene ontology (GO) terms related to transcriptional regulation, development, and differentiation.
claims.source: SCML2 targets were significantly enriched for gene ontology (GO) terms related to transcriptional regulation, development, and differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1A), as observed for targets of the Polycomb repressive machinery in other systems (Schuettengruber et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the GO analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: SCML2 and BMI1 co-occupied several promoters, including those of transcription factors RUNX1, IKZF2, and DMRT1.
claims.source: SCML2 and BMI1 co-occupied several promoters, including those of transcription factors RUNX1, IKZF2, and DMRT1 (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: SCML2 shared ∼46% of its target genes with BMI1.
claims.source: Overall, SCML2 shared ∼46% of its target genes with BMI1 (Figure 4F, Supplementary file 1B), almost four times more than expected by chance (p=2.5 × 10−119, hypergeometric distribution).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The overlap between SCML2 and BMI1 target genes was almost four times more than expected by chance (p=2.5 × 10−119).
claims.source: Overall, SCML2 shared ∼46% of its target genes with BMI1 (Figure 4F, Supplementary file 1B), almost four times more than expected by chance (p=2.5 × 10−119, hypergeometric distribution).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the statistical analysis of the overlap shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The overlap between SCML2 and BMI1 target genes became more pronounced as a function of decreasing p-values for the ERs.
claims.source: This overlap became more pronounced as a function of decreasing p-values for the ERs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E), suggesting that many of the SCML2-only or BMI1-only sites were false positives due to noise in the ChIP-seq signal.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E.

claims.claim: SCML2ΔRBR was lost from several target genes.
claims.source: Visual inspection of ChIP-seq profiles revealed that SCML2ΔRBR was lost from several target genes (Figure 5A), suggesting that the RBR, and presumably RNA–protein interactions might participate in the recruitment or stabilization of SCML2 on chromatin.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: A smaller number of SCML2 ERs exhibited SCML2AΔRBR levels comparable to WT.
claims.source: A smaller number of SCML2 ERs, including the ER near the RUNX1 TSS, exhibited SCML2AΔRBR levels comparable to WT (Figure 5A), consistent with the existence of RNA-independent pathways of SCML2A recruitment at some loci.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The N3–SCML2ΔRBR ChIP-seq signal was much weaker than WT when all significant ERs for SCML2 WT were combined in a single meta-ER plot.
claims.source: Nonetheless, RBR-independent ERs constituted a small proportion of the total SCML2 binding profile, because the N3–SCML2ΔRBR ChIP-seq signal was much weaker than WT when all significant (p<10−5 according to MACS 1.4.0rc2) ERs for SCML2 WT were combined in a single meta-ER plot (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the meta-ER plot shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Partial replacement of endogenous SCML2 with SCML2AΔRBR resulted in a decreased, albeit not abolished, accumulation of BMI1 at several of the target sites.
claims.source: Consistent with our observations that SCML2A colocalizes with BMI1 (Figure 4E,F) and can recruit it to chromatin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), partial replacement of endogenous SCML2 with SCML2AΔRBR resulted in a decreased, albeit not abolished, accumulation of BMI1 at several of the target sites (Figure 5A,C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A,C.

claims.claim: Out of 148 high-confidence ERs obtained from the triple intersection of SCML2, HA, and BMI1 ERs, a majority displayed losses in SCML2 binding in the absence of the RBR and many also had decreased BMI1 occupancy.
claims.source: When inspected at the level of individual genomic regions, out of 148 high-confidence ERs obtained from the triple intersection of SCML2, HA, and BMI1 ERs, a majority displayed losses in SCML2 binding in the absence of the RBR and many also had decreased BMI1 occupancy (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the heatmap shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: SCML2 is recruited to a subset of target genes through a process that requires its RNA-binding activity.
claims.source: From this set of experiments, we conclude that SCML2 is recruited to a subset of target genes through a process that requires its RNA-binding activity and that the presence of mutant SCML2AΔRBR that is not chromatin-bound causes a partial release of BMI1 and, presumably, PRC1 from chromatin.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the ChIP-seq experiments.

claims.claim: The presence of mutant SCML2AΔRBR that is not chromatin-bound causes a partial release of BMI1 and, presumably, PRC1 from chromatin.
claims.source: From this set of experiments, we conclude that SCML2 is recruited to a subset of target genes through a process that requires its RNA-binding activity and that the presence of mutant SCML2AΔRBR that is not chromatin-bound causes a partial release of BMI1 and, presumably, PRC1 from chromatin.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the ChIP-seq experiments.

claims.claim: Only in the case of WT SCML2A, RNA could be detected in the co-IP.
claims.source: To this end, we performed HA IPs in 293T-REx expressing N3-tagged SCML2A WT, ΔRBR, or the N3 tag alone. Although comparable amounts of WT and ΔRBR protein were recovered, only in the case of WT SCML2A, we could detect co-IP of RNA (Figure 6A,B), which we subjected to deep sequencing (RIP followed by sequencing, RIP-seq).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the RIP data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claims.claim: Several specific interactions distinguished the set of RNAs recovered in RIPs for SCML2A WT from all other controls.
claims.source: Although overall abundant lincRNAs were more likely to be detected by RIP-seq, several specific interactions distinguished the set of RNAs recovered in RIPs for SCML2A WT from all other controls (Figure 6C), demonstrating the specificity of RNA binding by SCML2 in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Cell differentiation caused a measurable shift in the pool of lincRNAs associated with SCML2.
claims.source: Indeed, cell differentiation caused a measurable shift in the pool of lincRNAs associated with SCML2 (Figure 6D), suggesting that in addition to intrinsic binding preferences, cellular context may also determine which RNAs bind to SCML2 and, in turn, how its function and distribution on chromatin is affected by these interactions.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the heatmap shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Several unannotated ncRNAs were enriched in SCML2 RIPs compared to input RNA and were transcribed near SCML2 ERs.
claims.source: We also found several examples of unannotated ncRNAs that were enriched in SCML2 RIPs compared to input RNA and were transcribed near SCML2 ERs (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–E), which is consistent with the notion that some ncRNAs interacting with SCML2 might act in cis.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the RIP-seq and ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-E.

claims.claim: SCML2 associates with annotated and unannotated lncRNAs via the RBR in vivo.
claims.source: Thus, SCML2 associates with annotated and unannotated lncRNAs via the RBR in vivo. These interactions are specific and they are also dynamic, likely reflecting the need to adjust SCML2 localization or regulation as the cells transition from one transcriptional and/or epigenetic state to another.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the RIP-seq experiments.

claims.claim: SCML2-RNA interactions are specific and dynamic.
claims.source: Thus, SCML2 associates with annotated and unannotated lncRNAs via the RBR in vivo. These interactions are specific and they are also dynamic, likely reflecting the need to adjust SCML2 localization or regulation as the cells transition from one transcriptional and/or epigenetic state to another.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the RIP-seq experiments.

claims.claim: A total of 530 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified after SCML2 knockdown using a cutoff of p<0.2.
claims.source: We generated genome-wide expression profiles by RNA-seq in two biological replicates and combined all data sets to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Using a loose cutoff of p<0.2, we identified a total of 530 DEGs of which a significant fraction overlapped (p=1.4 × 10−4, hypergeometric distribution) with the set of genes associated with an SCML2 ER (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: A significant fraction of DEGs after SCML2 knockdown overlapped with the set of genes associated with an SCML2 ER (p=1.4 × 10−4).
claims.source: We generated genome-wide expression profiles by RNA-seq in two biological replicates and combined all data sets to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Using a loose cutoff of p<0.2, we identified a total of 530 DEGs of which a significant fraction overlapped (p=1.4 × 10−4, hypergeometric distribution) with the set of genes associated with an SCML2 ER (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: A majority (341) of DEGs after SCML2 knockdown were upregulated.
claims.source: In keeping with the postulated repressive function of SCML2, a majority (341) of these genes were upregulated (Supplementary file 1C) and this subset accounted for ∼86% of the DEGs associated with SCML2 occupancy on chromatin (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Upregulated genes after SCML2 knockdown accounted for ∼86% of the DEGs associated with SCML2 occupancy on chromatin.
claims.source: In keeping with the postulated repressive function of SCML2, a majority (341) of these genes were upregulated (Supplementary file 1C) and this subset accounted for ∼86% of the DEGs associated with SCML2 occupancy on chromatin (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The levels of BMI1 on chromatin were unaffected after SCML2 knockdown, even at sites that lost SCML2 occupancy.
claims.source: Given that SCML2A can recruit BMI1, and therefore PRC1, to an artificial reporter and that PRC1 is generally thought as the effector of Polycomb-mediated repression (Simon and Kingston, 2009), we hypothesized that the changes in transcriptional activity observed above might be secondary to a loss of BMI1 from SCML2-bound genes. Unexpectedly, this was not the case. In fact, the levels of BMI1 on chromatin were unaffected even when we analyzed only the 520 sites that lost SCML2 occupancy after SCML2 knockdown (Figure 7D,E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claims.claim: In the absence of SCML2, PRC1 alone is not sufficient to maintain repression at all target genes.
claims.source: Together with the observation that SCML2B retains the ability to repress a reporter independent of BMI1 recruitment (Figure 4C), these findings reinforce the notion that SCML2 represses transcription by itself, and that, in its absence, PRC1 alone is not sufficient to maintain repression at all target genes.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq experiments.

claims.claim: SCML2 represses transcription by itself.
claims.source: Together with the observation that SCML2B retains the ability to repress a reporter independent of BMI1 recruitment (Figure 4C), these findings reinforce the notion that SCML2 represses transcription by itself, and that, in its absence, PRC1 alone is not sufficient to maintain repression at all target genes.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq experiments.

claims.claim: SCML2 and PRC1 cooperate in chromatin binding.
claims.source: Here, we have unveiled two mechanisms by which SCML2A contributes to PRC1 function: (1) SCML2 and PRC1 cooperate in chromatin binding, as evidenced by loss of BMI1 upon overexpression of SCML2AΔRBR, recruitment of BMI1 by SCML2A at artificial tethering sites, and the weak association of SCML2B to chromatin; and (2) SCML2 enforces repression at some target sites independent of the presence of PRC1.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claims.claim: SCML2 enforces repression at some target sites independent of the presence of PRC1.
claims.source: Here, we have unveiled two mechanisms by which SCML2A contributes to PRC1 function: (1) SCML2 and PRC1 cooperate in chromatin binding, as evidenced by loss of BMI1 upon overexpression of SCML2AΔRBR, recruitment of BMI1 by SCML2A at artificial tethering sites, and the weak association of SCML2B to chromatin; and (2) SCML2 enforces repression at some target sites independent of the presence of PRC1.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claims.claim: RNA binding plays a role in SCML2 function, as it is required for its localization to chromatin.
claims.source: In addition, our results show that RNA binding also plays a role in SCML2 function, as it is required for its localization to chromatin.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claims.claim: The interaction of SCM and PRC1 in Drosophila relies on the C-terminal SPM domain.
claims.source: In Drosophila, the interaction of SCM and PRC1 relies on the C-terminal SPM domain (Peterson et al., 2004) and our results show that a similar mechanism is conserved in humans.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: A similar mechanism of SCM-PRC1 interaction via the SPM domain is conserved in humans.
claims.source: In Drosophila, the interaction of SCM and PRC1 relies on the C-terminal SPM domain (Peterson et al., 2004) and our results show that a similar mechanism is conserved in humans.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the mass spectrometry data (Figure 4A).

claims.claim: SCML2 is part of PRC1.2, which does not contain BMI1.
claims.source: The former might reflect the complexity of PRC1 subtypes in mammals and the fact that SCML2 is also part of PRC1.2, which does not contain BMI1 (Gao et al., 2012); the latter is likely due to the higher sensitivity of the BMI1 antibody, although we cannot exclude that some BMI1 target sites are devoid of SCML2.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: SCML2 might directly enforce gene repression via the MBT domain, which binds to methylated histone tails.
claims.source: This PRC1-independent silencing may be mediated by the MBT domain, which binds to methylated histone tails (Grimm et al., 2007; Santiveri et al., 2008) and, in the case of L3MBTL1, represses transcription via chromatin compaction (Trojer et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation based on prior work on MBT domains.

claims.claim: The MBT domain of SCM in Drosophila is important for repression.
claims.source: In fact, the MBT domain of SCM in Drosophila is important for repression (Grimm et al., 2007), and our results show that the MBT domain contributes to the chromatin localization of SCML2 (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The MBT domain contributes to the chromatin localization of SCML2.
claims.source: In fact, the MBT domain of SCM in Drosophila is important for repression (Grimm et al., 2007), and our results show that the MBT domain contributes to the chromatin localization of SCML2 (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the salt fractionation data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The 74-residue fragment containing the RBR is both necessary and sufficient for RNA binding in vitro.
claims.source: Despite the fact that the 74-residue fragment containing the RBR is both necessary and sufficient for RNA binding in vitro (Figures 1 and 2), prediction algorithms failed to detect known protein folds or the propensity to form secondary structures in this region, suggesting that, in isolation, the RBR remains unstructured.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the in vitro binding data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: In isolation, the RBR remains unstructured.
claims.source: Despite the fact that the 74-residue fragment containing the RBR is both necessary and sufficient for RNA binding in vitro (Figures 1 and 2), prediction algorithms failed to detect known protein folds or the propensity to form secondary structures in this region, suggesting that, in isolation, the RBR remains unstructured.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on the failure of prediction algorithms to detect structure.

claims.claim: Induced fit is a common feature of RNA–protein interactions.
claims.source: This is not entirely unexpected, considering that induced fit is a common feature of RNA–protein interactions (Williamson, 2000).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The fragile X syndrome protein FMR1/FMRP contains an arginine-rich stretch that is disordered in solution but becomes ordered in presence of an RNA ligand.
claims.source: For example, the fragile X syndrome protein FMR1/FMRP contains an arginine-rich stretch that is disordered in solution but becomes ordered in presence of an RNA ligand (Phan et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The RBR was dispensable for the interaction with PRC1.
claims.source: Although the RBR was dispensable for the interaction with PRC1, its disruption resulted not only in a delocalization of SCML2A from chromatin (Figure 3), but also in decreased PRC1 occupancy at several target genes (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the mass spectrometry data (Figure 4A).

claims.claim: Disruption of the RBR resulted in delocalization of SCML2A from chromatin and decreased PRC1 occupancy at several target genes.
claims.source: Although the RBR was dispensable for the interaction with PRC1, its disruption resulted not only in a delocalization of SCML2A from chromatin (Figure 3), but also in decreased PRC1 occupancy at several target genes (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the fractionation and ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claims.claim: Nucleoplasmic SCML2ΔRBR might function in a dominant negative fashion, titrating PRC1 away from chromatin.
claims.source: This observation is intriguing in view of the fact that short-term SCML2 knockdown did not affect BMI1 localization, and suggests that nucleoplasmic SCML2ΔRBR, being still capable of interacting with BMI1 through the SPM domain, might function in a dominant negative fashion, titrating PRC1 away from chromatin.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on the observation that SCML2ΔRBR interacts with BMI1 but is not chromatin-bound.

claims.claim: SCML2–RNA interactions appeared to be specific in vivo.
claims.source: Despite promiscuous RNA binding in vitro, SCML2–RNA interactions appeared to be specific in vivo, as demonstrated by the following observations: (1) the profile of lincRNAs enriched in the SCML2A WT RIP-seq was unique and distinct from input and control samples (Figure 6C); (2) the lincRNAs associated with SCML2 changed upon cellular differentiation (Figure 6D); and (3) several divergently transcribed ncRNAs were enriched in SCML2 RIPs although the coding mRNAs originating from the same locus were not (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the RIP-seq data shown in Figures 6C-E.

claims.claim: Physical proximity on chromatin alone was not the main determinant of SCML2–RNA interactions.
claims.source: The latter also demonstrates that physical proximity on chromatin alone was not the main determinant of SCML2–RNA interactions.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the observation that divergent ncRNAs but not nearby mRNAs are enriched in SCML2 RIPs.

claims.claim: The RBR is likely required to mediate the interactions with RNAs in vivo.
claims.source: Furthermore, the RBR is likely required to mediate the interactions with these RNAs, given that immunoprecipitation of the ΔRBR mutant recovered less RNA than the WT (Figure 6B) and that the few detected ΔRBR-associated RNAs were undistinguishable from those obtained in empty tag-expressing cells (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the RIP data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claims.claim: The RBR of SCML2A contributes to its recruitment either by interacting with trans-acting RNAs transcribed from distant intergenic loci, or by recognizing cis-acting ncRNAs.
claims.source: We propose that the RBR of SCML2A contributes to its recruitment either by interacting with trans-acting RNAs transcribed from distant intergenic loci, or by recognizing cis-acting ncRNAs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed model based on the RIP-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Divergent and overlapping antisense ncRNAs that originate downstream of the TSS have a demonstrated role in gene regulation.
claims.source: The latter may include divergent and overlapping antisense ncRNAs that originate downstream of the TSS, some of which have a demonstrated role in gene regulation (Faghihi and Wahlestedt, 2009; Modarresi et al., 2012), or promoter-associated ncRNAs that originate near the TSS of coding genes and are transcribed from the same strand (Kapranov et al., 2007), similar to the ncRNAs reported to bind PRC2 via SUZ12 (Kanhere et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Promoter-associated ncRNAs originate near the TSS of coding genes and are transcribed from the same strand.

results.result: SCML2 contains a novel RNA-binding region (RBR) spanning amino acids 256–330 that is necessary and sufficient for RNA binding in vitro. The RBR exhibits little sequence specificity but discriminates between RNA and DNA, preferring single-stranded over double-stranded RNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C36–C41 collectively demonstrate the identification and characterization of the RBR through RIP experiments (C36), domain mapping (C38), and in vitro binding assays (C39–C41). The data from Figures 1A, 1C, and 1D provide converging evidence for the RBR's RNA-binding properties.

results.result: The RBR can form ternary complexes with nucleosomes and RNA simultaneously, with higher affinity for RNA than nucleosomes or DNA. The RBR shows some sequence/structure preference, binding full-length HOTAIR more efficiently than isolated stem-loops or 601 RNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C42–C51 are supported by EMSA experiments (Figure 2A–C) and pull-down assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) demonstrating ternary complex formation and binding preferences. The super-shifted band in Figure 2C and controls excluding GST-mediated dimerization (C47) provide strong evidence.

results.result: SCML2A is tightly associated with chromatin through coordinated action of multiple domains: the RBR (RNA binding), MBT domains (histone mark recognition), and SPM domain (PRC1 interaction). Deletion of the RBR or mutation of the MBT domain reduces chromatin association, with the RBR deletion having a stronger effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C52–C59 are supported by salt fractionation experiments (Figure 3A–D) showing differential chromatin association of wild-type and mutant proteins. The quantification in Figure 3C demonstrates statistically significant differences (p-values from 2-way ANOVA), and the observation holds across different expression levels.

results.result: SCML2A exhibits punctate nuclear localization consistent with recruitment to specific chromatin sites, while SCML2AΔRBR shows diffuse nuclear distribution. The number of intense GFP spots decreased from a median of 39 per cell for SCML2A to 5 per cell for SCML2AΔRBR.
results.evaluation: Claims C60–C62 are supported by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 3E–G) with quantification showing statistically significant differences (p<0.001, unpaired t-test). The microscopy data corroborate the biochemical fractionation results, providing orthogonal validation.

results.result: SCML2A binds to PRC1 via its SPM domain, as demonstrated by mass spectrometry showing that both SCML2AWT and SCML2AΔRBR co-purify with canonical PRC1 components (RING1A/B, CBX2/8, PHC2/3, BMI1), while SCML2B (lacking SPM) shows only trace PRC1 association. SCML2A also co-purifies with SCMH1 and L3MBTL3.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C64–C69 are supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 4A) and immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 4B). The observation that ΔRBR retains PRC1 binding (C65) while SCML2B does not (C66) demonstrates the SPM domain's role. USP7 co-purification serves as an appropriate positive control (C68).

results.result: Artificial tethering of both SCML2A and SCML2B to a reporter causes dose-dependent transcriptional repression. However, only SCML2A recruits BMI1 to the reporter, indicating that BMI1 recruitment is not necessary for SCML2-mediated repression in this context.
results.evaluation: Claims C70–C72 are supported by luciferase assays (Figure 4C) and ChIP-qPCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B). The data demonstrate that SCML2 has repressive activity independent of PRC1 recruitment, which is a key mechanistic finding. The dose-dependent response strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: SCML2 occupies chromatin at sites enriched near transcription start sites (>30% within 10 kb of TSS) of genes involved in transcriptional regulation, development, and differentiation. SCML2 shares ~46% of its target genes with BMI1, representing a highly significant overlap (p=2.5×10⁻¹¹⁹) that increases with more stringent p-value cutoffs.
results.evaluation: Claims C74–C79 are supported by ChIP-seq analysis (Figure 4D–F) with appropriate statistical testing (hypergeometric distribution). The GO enrichment analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and the observation that overlap increases with decreasing p-values (C79) strengthen confidence in the findings.

results.result: Deletion of the RBR reduces SCML2A occupancy at most target genes, though a smaller subset of sites retain SCML2AΔRBR at WT levels. Meta-analysis of all significant ERs shows much weaker SCML2ΔRBR signal compared to WT.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C80–C82 are supported by ChIP-seq comparing WT and ΔRBR (Figure 5A,B). The meta-ER plot (Figure 5B) provides genome-wide quantification, while individual loci (Figure 5A) show both RBR-dependent and RBR-independent sites. The observation is confirmed with additional biological replicates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).

results.result: Overexpression of SCML2AΔRBR causes decreased BMI1 occupancy at several target sites, suggesting that SCML2A contributes to PRC1 recruitment. Out of 148 high-confidence co-occupied sites, the majority show losses in both SCML2 and BMI1 binding when the RBR is deleted.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C9, C83–C86 are supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 5A,C,E) showing coordinate loss of SCML2 and BMI1 at many sites. However, the mechanism is complex: the ΔRBR mutant retains PRC1 binding in vitro (C65) but causes BMI1 loss on chromatin, suggesting a dominant-negative effect as discussed (C115).

results.result: SCML2 associates with annotated and unannotated lncRNAs via the RBR in vivo. RIP-seq shows specific interactions that distinguish SCML2AWT from controls and ΔRBR mutant. These interactions are dynamic, changing upon cellular differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C87, C88, C91–C92 are supported by RIP experiments (Figure 6A,B) and RIP-seq analysis (Figure 6C,D). The PCA analysis (Figure 6C) demonstrates specificity, and the differentiation experiments (Figure 6D) show dynamic changes. The requirement for the RBR is clearly demonstrated by the ΔRBR control.

results.result: Cell differentiation causes measurable shifts in the pool of lincRNAs associated with SCML2. Several unannotated ncRNAs enriched in SCML2 RIPs are transcribed near SCML2 enriched regions, suggesting potential cis-acting mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C89–C90 are supported by RIP-seq in differentiated K562 cells (Figure 6D) and examples of unannotated ncRNAs near SCML2 ERs (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–E). However, the authors note they could not detect genome-wide spatial correlation (C123), limiting the strength of the cis-acting hypothesis.

results.result: SCML2 knockdown results in 530 differentially expressed genes (p<0.2), with a significant fraction overlapping SCML2-bound genes (p=1.4×10⁻⁴). The majority (341) are upregulated, consistent with SCML2's repressive function, and upregulated genes account for ~86% of DEGs at SCML2-occupied sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C93–C96 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 7A–C), but the use of a loose p-value cutoff (p<0.2) is concerning and may include many false positives. The authors acknowledge this limitation by showing more stringent analysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), but the small number of genes with p<0.05 limits statistical power. The directional bias toward upregulation is consistent with repression, but the magnitude of effects and reproducibility across stringent cutoffs need consideration.

results.result: SCML2 knockdown causes gene derepression without affecting BMI1 chromatin occupancy, even at sites that lose SCML2. This demonstrates that SCML2 represses transcription independently of PRC1, and that PRC1 alone is insufficient to maintain repression at all target genes in SCML2's absence.
results.evaluation: Claims C97–C99 are supported by ChIP-seq for BMI1 after SCML2 knockdown (Figure 7D,E) showing maintained BMI1 levels despite SCML2 loss. Combined with the tethering data showing SCML2B represses without recruiting BMI1 (C72), this provides strong evidence for PRC1-independent repression. This is a key mechanistic finding distinguishing SCML2 function from simple PRC1 recruitment.

results.result: SCML2A contributes to PRC1 function through two mechanisms: (1) SCML2 and PRC1 cooperate in chromatin binding, and (2) SCML2 enforces repression at some target sites independent of PRC1 presence. RNA binding is required for SCML2 chromatin localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C100–C102 represent the authors' synthesis of their findings in the discussion. These conclusions are well-supported by the collective data: cooperation in chromatin binding is shown by BMI1 loss upon SCML2ΔRBR overexpression (C83–C84), PRC1-independent repression is shown by maintained repression without BMI1 recruitment (C72, C97–C99), and RNA-binding requirement is shown by fractionation and ChIP-seq of ΔRBR mutants (C55, C80–C82).

results.result: Background claims establishing the context of Polycomb group proteins, their complexes (PRC1, PRC2), recruitment mechanisms (PREs in Drosophila, limited understanding in mammals), and prior knowledge about SCM and its mammalian homologs SCMH1 and SCML2.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10–C35 are background statements supported by citations to prior literature. These establish the scientific context and rationale for the study. The citations appear appropriate and the statements accurately represent established knowledge in the field.

results.result: SCML2 does not co-precipitate with EZH2 or MLL. Deletion of the RBR does not affect nuclear import or interaction with PRC1 components.
results.evaluation: Claims C37 and C63 are supported by unpublished data (C37) and by the mass spectrometry showing ΔRBR retains PRC1 binding (C63, Figure 4A) plus microscopy showing nuclear localization (Figure 3F). These are important negative controls demonstrating specificity of SCML2-RNA interactions and that RBR deletion specifically affects chromatin binding rather than general protein function.

results.result: Discussion claims about conservation of SCM-PRC1 interaction mechanisms from Drosophila to humans, SCML2's participation in PRC1.2, potential mechanisms of MBT-mediated repression, and structural properties of the RBR including its likely unstructured nature and induced-fit binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C103–C112 are discussion points that synthesize the current findings with prior literature. The conservation claim (C103–C104) is supported by the mass spectrometry data. The PRC1.2 participation (C105) is cited from prior work. The MBT mechanism speculation (C106) is appropriately qualified as speculative. The RBR structural discussion (C109–C112) is reasonable inference from the binding data and failure of structure prediction algorithms.

results.result: The RBR is dispensable for PRC1 interaction in vitro, but its disruption causes SCML2A delocalization from chromatin and decreased PRC1 occupancy at target genes. The nucleoplasmic SCML2ΔRBR might function as a dominant negative, titrating PRC1 away from chromatin.
results.evaluation: Claims C113–C115 synthesize key observations: RBR-independent PRC1 binding (C113, supported by Figure 4A), but RBR-dependent chromatin localization and PRC1 recruitment (C114, supported by Figures 3 and 5). The dominant-negative hypothesis (C115) is speculative but reasonable given that ΔRBR retains PRC1 binding but is not chromatin-bound, and could explain why overexpression causes BMI1 loss while knockdown does not.

results.result: SCML2-RNA interactions are specific in vivo despite promiscuous binding in vitro, as demonstrated by unique RIP-seq profiles, differentiation-dependent changes, and selective enrichment of divergent ncRNAs over nearby mRNAs. Physical proximity on chromatin alone does not determine SCML2-RNA interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C116–C118 are discussion points well-supported by the RIP-seq data (Figure 6C–E). The three lines of evidence for specificity are clearly demonstrated. The conclusion about physical proximity (C117) is a reasonable inference from the observation that divergent ncRNAs but not nearby mRNAs are enriched.

results.result: The authors propose that the RBR contributes to SCML2A recruitment via trans-acting or cis-acting ncRNAs, including divergent antisense ncRNAs, overlapping antisense ncRNAs, or promoter-associated ncRNAs. However, genome-wide spatial correlation between RIP-seq and ChIP-seq signals could not be detected, possibly because only a subset of SCML2-associated ncRNAs act in cis.
results.evaluation: Claims C119–C124 represent a proposed model with acknowledged limitations. The examples of cis-acting ncRNAs (C90, Figure 6E) support the possibility, and the types of ncRNAs mentioned (C120–C122) are well-documented in the literature. However, the lack of genome-wide correlation (C123) is a significant limitation that weakens the cis-acting hypothesis. The explanation (C124) is speculative. This represents an interesting hypothesis requiring further validation.

results.result: The authors propose that SCML2A is retained at target genes through interaction with PRC1 and that SCML2A contributes to stabilizing PRC1.
results.evaluation: Claims C125–C126 represent a proposed model based on the collective findings. The retention via PRC1 interaction (C125) is supported by the SPM-dependent chromatin association (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–G) and co-localization data (Figure 4E,F). The stabilization of PRC1 (C126) is supported by the BMI1 loss upon SCML2ΔRBR overexpression (Figure 5). This is a reasonable synthesis of the data.

results.result: Both the MBT domains and the SPM domain contribute to the repressive activity of SCM in Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 is a statement about prior work in Drosophila, supported by appropriate citations. This provides context for interpreting the mammalian SCML2 data and supports the conclusion that SCML2 has intrinsic repressive activity beyond PRC1 recruitment.
